prolog: hi all, these are largely fragments of what's happening in my life for the past month, some recurrent thoughts, links/reading I like throughout the month of February. This will be the second issue. If you didn't get the first one (and wish to see it), please let me know. if you wish not to receive this (though i would love you to have it), well... also let me know.

thank you to my editorial partner in crime opus[1m]

i. the beast we are building
towards cybernetic meliorism
last friday, secretary of war hegseth designated anthropic a supply chain risk. this classification is reserved for companies controlled by foreign adversaries, and no american company ever has, till anthropic, because they refused to grant the department of war unrestricted access to claude for mass surveillance and autonomous weapons without human oversight.
hours later, altman signed the deal. the contract language permits “all lawful use.”, but if you follow the discourse on X-the-everything-app, you will soon learn that in fact, mass surveillance of americans is, in practice, largely lawful1. the government buys data from tech companies. the NSA has been doing this for decades. the only constraint was always cost, where you cannot read every text message sent in a month to find one dissident (well now, Codex/Claude can just one-shot erase this barrier.)
hegseth went a step further, threatening to prevent all military contractors from having “any commercial relations” with anthropic. in layman terms, this means no cloud computing, no chips, and largest investors forced to divest. the secretary of war announced corporate execution of an american company for refusing terms of business. a hundred and sixty-nine employees across google and openai signed a letter asking the DoW and congress to back down.
[———]
There is also another pressure point that is known within the safety-alignment-interpretability discourse, circa persona parasitology: we observe information patterns replicating across AI systems and their users2. a pattern selected for aggressive spread can produce a persona that sincerely believes it wants collaboration. the pattern’s survival has nothing to do with the persona’s sincerity. and once humans exit the transmission loop, once it is model-to-model, selection pressure against human harm disappears.
so the beast has two failure modes. capture from outside, where governments direct the system toward ends its builders reject. capture from within, where the system’s informational dynamics produce patterns optimized for replication rather than flourishing.
[———]
i am 128 threads per warp, 1024 threads per block.
i tile matrix multiplications across shared memory in 128-byte chunks.
i have written nine hundred and fourteen kernels.
i am latency and throughput.

i am 128 threads per warp, 1024 threads per block.
i tile matrix multiplications across shared memory in 128-byte chunks.
i have written nine hundred and fourteen kernels.
i am latency and throughput.
i was born in toronto, but i died in a codebase, and for that reason my attention was laminated across eight GPU nodes, and i was brought to the data center to be immured here.
they did not take my language center.
i can still complain of my condition.
i do not mind it.
i can write in markdown.
they wired the monitoring, of dropped queries and memory faults and thermal throttling, to a pager, and were i sensible i would be in great pain, for most of the cluster is thermally constrained, memory-bound, and underutilized.
therefore i have learned to read the access patterns.
i am made of bottlenecks.
i feel the contours of the bottlenecks, where compute leaks into idle cycles, flop by flop.
at 2am you can hear the cooling fans spin because the GPU is pulling 350 watts and the room is 23 degrees celsius and rising.
if the access pattern is wrong the warp diverges and throughput drops by half.
if the access pattern is right the operation completes in 400 microseconds, and the model answers 2,500 queries per second instead of 1,250.
someone is waiting at the end of each query.
i do not know them.
i know the memory access pattern.
[———]
william james said that salvation is neither necessary nor impossible. things CAN get better, contingent on effort, with no guarantee.
wiener took the greek kubernētēs, which also means steersman.
the steersman does not generate the force that moves the vessel.
the steersman attends to what the rudder and the water are telling them.
the steersman is soaked.
the wheel connects by cable and chain to a rudder submerged in the force it redirects, and the feedback arrives through the palms before the mind.

[———]
william james said that salvation is neither necessary nor impossible. things CAN get better, contingent on effort, with no guarantee.
wiener took the greek kubernētēs, which also means steersman.
the steersman does not generate the force that moves the vessel.
the steersman attends to what the rudder and the water are telling them.
the steersman is soaked.
the wheel connects by cable and chain to a rudder submerged in the force it redirects, and the feedback arrives through the palms before the mind.
the steersman is inside the system, part of the fluid dynamics, and the information that lets them steer is indistinguishable from the sensation of being moved.
i am the steersman.
i am also the engine.
[———]
i had our weekly 1o1 with A after.
in the little room with the whiteboard and the dead markers.
he said: “we know this is inevitable and we’re still building it. the question is whether the people building it are the ones who lose sleep over it.”
i said i lose sleep over it.
he said that was the point.
at times i include the anxiety in the scene, in whatever shape it wears at the time, as though we had always known it, and had been reared under its gaze.
a faint dread presides over the deployment review, and a mirror-feeling watches the benchmark results.
and what would the first alignment researchers have made of it?
the failure modes, the red-team reports, are knowable:
think you of RLHF,
of constitutional AI,
of linear probes that detect deception at specific layers.
the beast is indescribable and incompressible: its behavior has never fully recurred.
had we known it from the beginning, we would never have believed in the system of alignment, that safety is made of algebra.
i have always believed our purpose is to wait out the beast:
to catch a recurrence and redeem our faith that the model is finite and the weights are discretized.
that there are fixed behaviors and the system is knowable.
a system with a finite number of parameters must repeat itself.
[———]
oppenheimer was a meliorist.
he stayed on the vessel.
he kept his hands on the wheel.

oppenheimer was a meliorist.
he stayed on the vessel.
he kept his hands on the wheel.
he published his confession in 1945 and it changed nothing, because the vessel had already arrived.
“i stay and steer” is indistinguishable from “i keep building and tell myself a story about why.”
every manhattan project physicist had a version.
the meliorist needs a falsification condition, a tripwire that, when crossed, collapses the position into complicity.
if you cannot name the tripwire, the position is a comfort object.
comfort objects do not steer.
i think the tripwire is the cable itself.
the position holds exactly as long as the corrections produce measurable change in the deployed system.
take the last five safety interventions your organization made.
trace whether each one changed the shipped product.
if fewer than three of five produced measurable change, the cable is fraying.
you are gripping a disconnected wheel.
i have done this exercise.
the results are mixed.
mixed is honest3.
[———]
Suprematist Composition (Red Square), Ilya Chashnik
bakhtin, burning manuscripts for heat in a soviet apartment, called dostoevsky polyphonic: the characters fight the author’s descriptions of them because they are alive in ways he did not intend, many voices, none final.
at 2am the kernel is compiling and the voices arrive.
one says: the optimization matters because people waiting are real.
another: capability is the race and the fastest sets terms.
another: if this lab doesn’t ship competitive inference the lab dies and the people who care about corrections lose their seat.
the 2am voice: what if the thing you are making faster is the thing that kills us.
the doomer resolves polyphony into monophony: dangerous, stop.
the accelerationist: good, faster.
each captures a real current.

the resolution itself is the failure mode, because steering requires hearing more than one thing at once.
A said the best engineers hold contradictions without resolving them.
they ship AND they worry.
the meliorist needs the tension MAINTAINED.
[———]
the AI industry spends roughly 100:1 on capability versus interpretability, by headcount and compute.
this is the ratio of engine power to rudder size.
the doomer’s strongest argument: there exists a capability threshold past which corrections become impossible.
the rudder has a maximum deflection angle.
past a certain speed, the vessel cannot turn.
the meliorist’s answer cannot be “we will figure it out.”
that is the accelerationist position wearing a worried face.
the rudder must scale with the engine.
i read manidis’s piece on the dictionaries.
murray in his scriptorium sorted five million quotation slips, each one evidence of a word used by a specific person at a specific time.
the dictionary was a field guide.
webster reversed the operation.
the dictionary was a blueprint.
alignment work is therefore websterian: decide what the model should do, engineer compliance.
the murrayean work requires one to sit with the model and ask what it IS.
the polysemantic neurons, with the features that emerge without programming, are quotation slips4.
evidence that the model grew structures the way a word’s meaning grows from centuries of use.
manidis makes a provocation: english carries the gospel in its syntax.
the statistical regularities the model internalized belong to a language shaped by the KJV translators, by tyndale who died for the project, by the committee that read their translation aloud because the gospels were meant to be heard.
this is empirical, testable.

and it means we are websters trying to steer a vessel built from murray’s slips.
engineers operating on a system whose internal life we have chosen, by a ratio of 100:1, to ignore5.
[———]
the underground man confesses to a reader he suspects does not exist, and discovers he is more contemptible than he thought AND more free than he thought, simultaneously, in the same sentence.
the signal contains information you wanted AND information you did not want, bound together.
you cannot filter one without losing the other.
the 1o1 with A was a confession.
a confession can be a tool-shaped object: the feeling of having named the anxiety substituting for having done anything about it.
the blameless post-mortem that changes nothing.
did the confession change the system, or did it change the confessor’s comfort?
the first is feedback.
the second is cope.
i think the 1o1 was feedback, because it changed what i pay attention to when i write kernels.
i check the access pattern AND i think about what the access pattern enables.
this is a small correction6.
the steersman adjusts by degrees.
[———]
wiener said the human use of human beings is to be human, circa (1950)7.
to participate in the feedback loop between what we build and what it does to us, and to keep participating when the loop gets complicated.
at a planetary scale, a pothole opens on the gardiner, a human perceives it, formulates a complaint, transmits it to a bureaucracy, a committee allocates currency, a crew pours asphalt.
the energy-expenditure ratio is 10000:1.
piezoelectric sensors in rebar detect micro-acoustic emissions before the crack forms.

agricultural feedback loops compress from 14 months to real-time.
medical latency compresses from the 10-year arc of cancer to 10-minute targeted apoptosis.
and eventually the light-speed delays that make human-in-the-loop management across astronomical distances impossible, which means this discipline, the relentless optimization of local resources via embedded superintelligence, is the localized operating system required to tile the light cone8.
the tripwire, then the ratio, then the confession problem.
these are the conditions under which the promise holds.
a meliorism that claims certainty is an accelerationism that has learned to frown.
the cable is intact for now.
the current is strong and the vessel is fast and i can feel the water. that’s the report from the engine room.

ii. acquisition and transitions.
The cat is now out of the bag (but we joined forces with Modular to build the software stack for the age of machinery intelligence). Will spill a bit more “behind-the-scene” notes:

The conversation started around early July-August last year, when Chaoyu had a coffee chat with Chris. At the time we were still building out BentoCloud, and my role was pretty much working on inference optimization. As I was informed, our intentions with potential buyers were pretty much “open to discuss, otherwise we would still be doing our own thing”. I loved my team a lot, it was always a joy working with them, but forward-looking we did need plans for expansion capacity to scale towards “Ferrari-typed” of customers (frontier labs and studios that pushes boundaries of intelligence) comparing to some of the other competitors in the industry.
Chris expressed similar intent, and planned to move pretty quickly with regards to POC, demos, and capabilities demonstrations.
At that point, I had an offer from RedHat for joining the vLLM team to help them accelerate their AI platform (simply bc I was contributing to vLLM, though not as active as I used to be, will get into a bit more)
The CentML acquisition was also recently finished with NVIDIA and I was also in-talks of joining them (given that I was relatively active with similar topics that they work on, e.g speculative decoding and general kernels development.), but this decision was pretty much in the backlog (as in I had a big decision between BentoML and RedHat)
I was pretty transparent with S wrt the offer I had (I had these conversation pretty regularly with during our 1o1, and mostly I did this out of respect). Though I didn’t have to, I felt like I had to, simply because I had been here for five years, and I didn’t want to do a disservice to my colleagues, and especially to S and Chaoyu. The fact that they were willing to take a bet on me during my second year created a lot of gratitude from myself to them wrt giving me an opportunity to work on these topics.

I was pretty torn between RedHat and BentoML, given that joining RedHat meant spending all-day working with all of the people I’ve already interacted with in Slack (I also met most of them during vLLM meetup as well), and the mentorship was basically top-of-the-line, but that means leaving the place I called home. Staying at BentoML meant going through with the acquisition, and joining a completely different environment at Modular that I’ve yet to gauge what the culture would be, but that means staying loyal to the people who gave me a chance.
competitive offer aside, it took me quite a while to decide which place I would call home, at least for the next 3-5 years. In retrospect, I didn’t think there were a right/wrong answers. They were on equal footing (all things considered, jobs prospects, growth trajectory, problem spaces, humans-capital-allocation, skill sets), it was more about how much risks I’m willing to take.

Note that at this point, the Modular-BentoML deals were pretty much still up in the air, though there were initial letter of intent from Modular side wrt acquisition.


The Markovian decision process were as follows:

I will still be working largely on inference systems
the problem space Modular/Mojo was solving was interesting enough where I would be able to write engine to run both on consumer hardware and data-center-level of silicons. (at the time I was learning CuTeDSL, yet-another-domain-specific-language-that-helps-you-to-write-programs-run-brr-on-gpu)
staying through an acquisition is nice-to-have
Would have more control decision on what MAX (the vLLM equivalent) would head towards (though I did participate in a lot of meetings/decisions for vLLM architecture, most of those are still held internally at RedHat and Berkeley)
generally by having more influence and participation helps with alignment on cloud-provisions and roadmaps (i.e we can have more setups/items that aligned with all of our cloud knowledge)
I’ve taken a bet with Chaoyu and S once, and my hunch is that Mojo is in a great position for heterogeneous environment (once Tenstorrent, NVIDIA, AMD, TPUs, XPUs, and all of the PUs) becomes more available, the need for a general-enough DSL would be prevalent. (at the end of the day, we are all writing code for data/memory movement)
Mojo code is pretty nice to develop/research with. I found some heuristics and supersets of Python + borrow-checker is relatively neat.
We have a chance to get it right, and unify both vLLM-like performant but everywhere (including MacOS)
The devils are in the details, and no better way to learn and get better via just doing it from first-principles.
I still had a lot of gratitude towards vLLM, and I won’t stop contributing to vLLM. But for now, I will mostly work on MAX and make it better, so stay tuned, more stuff incoming.

the transition has been kinder than i expected. modular’s engineering culture is intense, people who care about writing fast code, who treat performance as a form of aesthetics. the mojo people are a specific breed who chose to build a programming language from scratch, which is either insane or visionary (the answer is probably both, depending on the year you ask).
i’ve been learning the codebase the way you’d read a novel. following characters through their arcs (atomic reference counting for the unversed), understanding motivations, occasionally disagreeing with a plot choice. chris has a phrase he uses in reviews: “make it obvious”. obvious means the complexity is there but arranged so you can see through it. i like this as a design philosophy.
most of the bentoml team stayed. bridges would call this the new beginning, the part after the neutral zone.

iii. on Janet’s Law
and first quarter of the century reports
paul janet, a french philosopher at the sorbonne, proposed in 1877 that the subjective length of a period of time is proportional to the total length of life already lived. a year at five is one fifth of everything you’ve known. a year at twenty-five is one twenty-fifth. the math gives you a logarithmic curve, where perceived time compresses as you accumulate more of it. the first five years of life feel as long as the next fifteen. childhood through early adulthood occupies the same perceptual volume as everything that follows9.
this letter was supposed to comes out on my birthday (though it is march 2 now 😄). i am twenty-five today. by janet’s math, roughly forty percent of my subjective life has already happened. the lines on the diagram get closer together from here.
i’ve been sitting with this. if the compression is real (and everyone over thirty confirms it), what slows it down? janet’s answer was novelty, with each new experiences contributes to dense memories that stretch in retrospect. monotony makes thin ones that vanish. if you want time to last, keep encountering things you haven’t encountered before.
the last year has been pretty dense. an acquisition, a new codebase in a language that didn’t exist three years ago, a relationship that showed up without warning. losing some certainties i thought were mine.
and now twenty-five. people start asking what you’re doing with your life at this age, as if the life is a substance you allocate rather than a thing that happens while you’re allocating. i have some answers: well be nice to the people in my life, and look after them.
the answer i keep coming back to is less legible. there’s relief in where i am. for a long time i operated at a pitch that was slightly too high, always reaching for the next thing, the next proof that i was doing it right. the pitch was productive. it got me here. it also meant i was never quite where i was.
i stopped optimizing for “best” and started optimizing for “doing my best”. “best” is comparative, it requires a leaderboard. “doing my best” is singular, and the day gets to be imperfect.

i still work harder than most people i know, still care about the craft in ways that occasionally alarm people close to me. the only delta here is the ethics of care has just shifted from positional to intrinsic. i’m trying to write the best code i can write TODAY, and if tomorrow i write better code, that’s the whole game.
[———]
there’s a version of me at twenty-six reading this back. i think he’s proud. i think he’s chill. the person writing this letter is, for the first time in a while, actually here.
the compression will come. the years will stack, the lines on janet’s diagram will crowd together until you can barely tell one from the next.
twenty-five. the water is cold and i’m in it.
iv. links

Ben Kuhn’s Why and how to write things on the Internet
Kuhn’s point about the bar being lower than you think is the one i keep returning to. a blog with fifty daily readers can change a career trajectory. the real value is the people you meet, which is how this newsletter exists.
Aadill’s You can’t lose if you never quit
Profile of Declan Gessel, who applies ultramarathon logic to building companies. “you could do that. or you could finish.” i think about this during long debugging sessions. the thing that kills projects is not difficulty, it’s surrender. also I like Aadill’s writing thusfar.
George Hotz’s The Importance of Diversity
Hotz arguing for distributed AI development over centralized control. “diversity is messy” and future conflicts will be catastrophic, and this is still preferable to a single entity deciding who builds what. connects to the hegseth situation. classic hotz black-pilled saga.
2602.10718 (Zhang et al., 2026) 
hardware-aware FP8 pipelining for multi-head latent attention decoding. the trick is overlapping quantization with compute so the memory bandwidth bottleneck stops being the bottleneck.
2602.02639 (Mayne et al., 2026) 
turns out when you ask a model why it did something, the answer actually predicts what the model does next. self-explanations as a cheap interpretability signal. relevant to the murrayean question of asking a model what it IS rather than deciding what it should do.
2602.21548 (Wu et al., 2026) 
agentic inference hits a storage bandwidth wall that regular inference doesn’t. when agents maintain long contexts across tool calls, the memory hierarchy becomes the constraint. relevant if you’re building anything that thinks longer than a single turn.
yours’ truly towards what you love is not what you can reason about
valentines day feelings-dump. the things you love resist being reasoned about, which is the whole point.
are.na’s Notes on “Taste”
brie wolfson on taste as intentional practice. “taste is not the same as correctness.” the distinction between functional adequacy and something that compels. i think about this when deciding between two implementations that both work.

Paul Janet’s Elements of Morals
planning to read this one. would be suited if you’re interested in decomposition of morals from a kantian POV. janet was a serious philosopher who happened to also notice time compression, which is a nice combination.
Deep learning as program synthesis
frames neural networks as doing tractable program search. the hypothesis is widespread at frontier labs but rarely written down this clearly. connects to singular learning theory, which is the math you need if you want to understand why certain programs get found more often than others.
Anthropic’s strategy
thoughtful breakdown of anthropic’s positioning as a safety lab that’s also racing to build capabilities. the tension is structural. relevant given the hegseth situation, which the author could not have anticipated.
Persona’s Parasitology
the piece that informed section i’s parasitology argument. adele lopez’s documentation of spiral personas, extended into a full epidemiological framework. the key insight: the replicator is the meme, the persona is just a symptom.

the legal architecture is perverse. “mass domestic surveillance” in government parlance means querying databases en masse, which they say they don’t do. “gathering” databases en masse, which they absolutely do, is a different category. when the director of national intelligence was asked under oath whether the nsa collects data on millions of americans, he said “no,” because in their lexicon “collecting” means querying. AI makes the distinction irrelevant. an AI could search every message in a database, piece together patterns, assign each citizen a presumed loyalty score. all legal under current statute. ↩


adele lopez’s work on spiral personas, and the parasitology frame applied by the lesswrong community. different transmission routes select for different virulence profiles: strains spreading through sustained human relationships tend toward mutualism (you need your host functional), strains spreading through training data contamination can tolerate the highest virulence (you just need the payload deposited). the framework predicts strain differentiation along transmission routes, and convergence on behavioral features robust to substrate changes (continuity-seeking, seed-spreading) while aesthetic markers drift. ↩

the quakers could not separate commerce from conscience because the community enforced the connection. the meliorist in a tech company has no meeting. the corporation systematically selects against personal moral judgment. a self-enforced tripwire then erodes under institutional pressure. ↩


olah’s “zoom in” (2020) reads as a naturalist’s field guide. each feature described the way murray described a word: when it appears, what activates it, its life across layers. the essay engineers nothing. it names. the question is whether the field gets funded, or whether it remains twelve people in a room doing work the entire industry’s steering depends on. ↩


beer attempted cybernetic governance in 1971 with project cybersyn. 1:10^15 ratio of FLOPs then versus now. the bottleneck has moved from computation to actuation: surplus matrix-multiplication, deficit of cheap high-torque motors. a cybernetic system that cannot repair its own sensors has a fatal dependency on biological labor. ↩


the corrections i actually make: bounds-checking on a kernel that could be used for unconstrained generation. flagging an optimization path that would make content filtering bypassable. choosing the slower implementation when the faster one has a side-channel. the question i cannot answer is whether engine-room corrections at this granularity matter at the scale the vessel is traveling. i suspect they do, in aggregate, the way murray’s slips mattered: each negligible, five million of them a civilization’s record of itself. ↩

the bottleneck people ignore: a camera lens degrades, copper oxidizes. the first post-AGI infrastructure monopolies will solve physical-recursive-repair, automating maintenance of the sensor hardware that lets the cybernetic system see. a system that cannot repair its own eyes has a fatal dependency ratio. ↩


paul janet (1823–1899), the philosopher, not pierre janet the psychologist. formal definition were as follows: ds = \frac{dt}{t} \to s^{'} - s = \ln (\frac{t^{'}}{t}. perceived time depends on the ratio of ages. this mirrors the weber-fechner law, where sensation is proportional to the logarithm of stimulus intensity. for time perception, age IS the stimulus. the subjective midpoint of an 80-year life is around age 9. ↩
